title: Some ports you walk off into. Most you don't.
subtitle: The itinerary prints a city's name. What it books is a berth, and the two are often an hour apart.

kicker: Read the berth, not the name
text: The port on your itinerary is not always the place on your itinerary.
sub: Civitavecchia is not Rome. Livorno is not Florence. Kuşadası is not Ephesus. Each of those is a scheduled coach ride before the day begins.

left.label: Walk off
items: Valletta — a lift and you're up
Chania — the harbour is the point

right.label: Plan ahead
items: Le Havre — Paris is a day trip

title: Four questions before any port day

items.head: How far is the thing from the berth?
items.body: Under twenty minutes on foot and you need no plan at all. Over an hour by road and you need a good one.

items.head: Alongside, or tendered?
items.body: Tendering adds a queue at each end and a weather clause you cannot argue with.

items.head: How long is the call, in ship's time?
items.body: Under seven hours alongside, the inland option stops being a choice and becomes a gamble.

items.head: How many ships share the day?
items.body: Two large ships alongside changes the town completely between nine and noon.

text: Sometimes the right plan is to skip the famous inland thing.
sub: Rome does not fit inside a port call, and pretending otherwise buys you four hours on a coach and ninety minutes of queue. Do Rome properly, before or after the ship.

quote: An itinerary is a list of berths. My job is telling you which of them are actually the places you meant to visit.

title: Send this to the person planning your shore days
body: Or send me a sailing you're weighing. I'll come back with which calls you can walk off into and which two need a plan made in advance.
